extracted.intended_audience: college mathematics faculty, curriculum designers, and math educators developing quantitative literacy/core competency courses
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and standards for designing, teaching, and assessing an undergraduate quantitative literacy / core competency mathematics course emphasizing problem solving, interpretation of quantitative information, and use of accessible technology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimal competency in mathematics (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: As a definition for minimal competency in mathematics at NIU, the Department proposed it consist of some computational facility and knowledge of elementary facts, facility at the interpretation of quantitative information, facility with elementary mathematical reasoning, and facility in problem solving.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Graduates should be able to use mathematics in their lives and be able to solve problems, accurately and comfortably estimate answers to problems, judge the reasonableness of an answer to a problem, read charts and graphs, and ask meaningful questions concerning quantitative information presented to them. The level expected should be commensurate with the intellectual development of a college student, while presupposing only intermediate algebra and geometry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Course prerequisites and level
rubrics_metrics.description: The course is college-level but presupposes only intermediate algebra and geometry as prerequisites.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because many students may have taken prerequisite material years earlier, the course design should consider whether review is necessary. Students may need activation of prior knowledge in context of problem settings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statistics content requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Include a substantial statistics component (about one third of the course) covering graphical presentation of data, measures of central tendency and dispersion, the normal curve, sampling, probability, and the nature of statistical testing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statistics topics should be taught with emphasis on interpreting and reasoning with real data and applications (e.g., governmental standards, medical tests, survey analysis).

rubrics_metrics.name: Logical reasoning content
rubrics_metrics.description: Include logical reasoning: inductive and elementary forms of deductive reasoning, the nature of valid arguments, common logical fallacies, and some survey analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teach students to recognize valid/invalid arguments and common fallacies and to apply inductive/deductive thought to real examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geometry and spatial reasoning in problem solving
rubrics_metrics.description: Include geometry in problem solving: geometrical notions of length, area, and volume; graphical solution of polynomial equations; systems of equations and inequalities; and study of spatial relationships.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use geometry to support solutions of practical problems encountered in everyday life (e.g., area/volume estimates, spatial optimization).

rubrics_metrics.name: Algebraic analysis and functions
rubrics_metrics.description: Include algebraic topics: algebraic analysis of polynomial equations, systems of linear equations, inequalities, the function concept, average rate of change, and some error analysis (especially relative error).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present these concepts in applied contexts and interleave with problem settings rather than as isolated mechanics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Estimation, approximation, and judging reasonableness
rubrics_metrics.description: Teach estimation, approximation, and strategies for judging the reasonableness of answers as an explicit course component.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repeatedly incorporate percentage change, orders of magnitude, and relative-error thinking into diverse problems to develop judgment skills.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem solving framework and Polya strategies
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide a general framework for problem solving (e.g., Polya’s How to Solve It) and explicitly teach problem-solving strategies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include a culminating unit illustrating Polya’s framework with problems from earlier sections; emphasize translating prose problems into mathematical formulation and multi-step solutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of accessible technology
rubrics_metrics.description: Build the course around technology all students can be expected to have and use—e.g., simple calculators and spreadsheet software (Excel).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use technology to create graphs/charts, carry out computations, and emphasize ideas over computation. Provide Excel instructions along with activities so students learn details 'almost without realizing it.' In activity design use features like absolute references ($) when teaching spreadsheet formulas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Activity-based pedagogy with pre-reading
rubrics_metrics.description: Intertwine background reading with carefully constructed in-class activities; students are expected to read background materials before topics are introduced in class.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Most class time spent on students working on activities while instructor circulates, answers questions, and gives occasional mini-lectures. Activities often require investigation and written analysis with interpretative explanations; encourage pair or small-group discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment mix (exams, quizzes, homework, projects)
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate students not only by hour examinations and a final examination, but also by homework performance, weekly quiz scores, and project work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weekly quizzes usually include a question that expects explanation in writing. Use at least two group projects (statistical test project and a personal business decisions project) with an individual written report required from each student for each project.

rubrics_metrics.name: Written communication requirement for activities
rubrics_metrics.description: Students are required to write up their analysis for each activity, 'complete with interpretative explanations of their results'; written assignments generally require at least a full paragraph.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Early in the course students may write short phrases and incomplete explanations, but expectation is progression to clear and appropriate narratives (80% of students achieved this by end of term in reported data).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid artificial situations; emphasize relevance
rubrics_metrics.description: To facilitate transfer into student lives, the teacher must avoid artificial situations and ensure the course is seen as relevant by students.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model the problem solving framework throughout instruction and mention it explicitly early. An upbeat attitude and appreciation for mathematics of everyday life promote positive student experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accommodate diverse learning styles and limited faculty resources
rubrics_metrics.description: Design the course to accommodate students with diverse learning styles and varying mathematical backgrounds; course delivery may need a master teacher in large-group meetings supplemented by small-group problem hours led by graduate teaching assistants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect that many students may have weaker backgrounds and may bring anxiety or distaste for math; provide contextual review and varied instructional modes (lecture, activities, projects).

rubrics_metrics.name: Course materials and exercises should emphasize non-mechanical, real-life problems
rubrics_metrics.description: Use or create texts/materials that present problems in prose form, include routine and nonroutine problems, and avoid overly mechanical exercises.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Problems should often require multi-step reasoning, problem formulation from incomplete/extra information, and repeated exposure to concepts across contexts; include examples that motivate students (e.g., personal finance, consumer decisions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of pre/post assessment instruments
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess both skills and attitudes using pre/post instruments such as attitude questionnaires and standardized tests (Wonderlic Basic Skills test).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Administer attitude questionnaires at start and end of course; use paired-sample comparisons to detect statistically-significant improvements in areas such as experience/confidence using spreadsheets, WWW for reliable data, spreadsheet/statistical software, and quantitative skills (grade level), algebra/geometry, applied problem solving, and interpretative problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Program success metrics (completion rate and student outcomes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure program success with metrics like course completion rate and improvement in student-written explanations, confidence, and skill levels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: in reported implementation, completion rate was 93% (71 enrolled, 4 withdrew, 3 failed) and 80% of students produced clear and appropriate narrative explanations by term end; use similar metrics to evaluate effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Activity design and student deliverable rubric (example: Ranking Cities)
rubrics_metrics.description: Design activities that require clear procedural steps, justification, use of technology, and interpretation. (Example activity required: rank cities on characteristics using a 1–10 scale; assign weights 1–10; compute weighted sums in Excel using formulas with absolute references; list top/bottom cities; discuss additional characteristics and advantages/disadvantages of the method.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For such activities require: a) explanation of cutoff decisions and rationale; b) clear column headings and recorded rankings; c) explanation of ranking rationale; d) weights entered and rationale explained; e) correct Excel formula usage (including $ for absolute references) and dragging down for all rows; f) reporting of highest/lowest weighted sums; g) discussion of other applicable decisions and pros/cons of method.
